item.title: Top House Oversight Dem demands answers to Trump’s media ban
item.description: “The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press, not freedom from criticism,” Robert Garcia writes.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, speaks to reporters about Leon Black, a billionaire who was close with Jeffrey Epstein, and who walked out of an investigative interview with the panel last June, at the Capitol in Washington on Sept. 16, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jalen Beckford
item.content:encoded:
The ranking Democrat on the House Oversight committee is demanding the White House answer questions related to President Donald Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House, calling it the president’s “most blatant, assault on press freedom.”

In a letter sent Monday to White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) requested that Cheung provide by Oct. 5 a detailed account of when and how he was informed of the ban, how he responded, who was consulted before the decision, the legal justification for it, the facts the White House relied on and whether the outlets had any opportunity to respond.

“The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press, not freedom from criticism,” wrote Garcia. “The American people need to understand what consideration—if any—the White House gave to this serious and unprecedented decision to protect the President’s ego.”

Garcia also asked for all White House staff documents and communications about the ban and for any other relevant materials to be preserved.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump on Friday announced that he was seeking to block journalists from POLITICO, MS NOW and CNN from the White House, complaining about “constant ‘reporting’” of what he called “FICTION and LIES.” The Trump administration first denied the media outlets entry into the White House grounds on Saturday morning.

The three news organizations are now jointly suing Trump, Cheung and two other top advisers in a bid to immediately restore access for their reporters, calling the ban a “direct assault on the First Amendment.”

Daniel Lippman contributed to this report.

item.title: OpenAI president and MAGA Inc. donor to attend Trump-Xi state dinner
item.description: OpenAI President Greg Brockman is expected to join a host of other tech executives at the dinner.

media:content.media:title: OpenAI president Greg Brockman speaks during an AMD news conference ahead of the annual Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 5, 2026. (Photo by Caroline Brehman / AFP via Getty Images)

item.dc:creator: By Sophia Cai and Cheyenne Haslett
item.dc:contributor: By Sophia Cai and Cheyenne Haslett
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI President Greg Brockman is expected to attend President Donald Trump’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House this week, according to a person with direct knowledge of the plans and a spokesperson for OpenAI who were were granted anonymity to discuss the arrangements.

Brockman was not included on an initial, partial list of tech and business leaders that a senior U.S. official provided to reporters on Friday. That list of expected attendees included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

The senior U.S. official described the dinner as “a very popular and hot ticketed event.”

Brockman and other Silicon Valley executives’ participation comes as the White House is grappling with national security concerns related to the AI industry and specifically ensuring the U.S. remains competitive with China. The White House has repeatedly said its posture on the topic is focused on preserving American leadership while managing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful systems.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Brockman and his wife, Anna, gave a combined $25 million to MAGA Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC, in 2025, according to campaign finance records. The contribution made the couple among the largest individual donors to Trump’s political operation. The donations were made in a personal capacity and not on behalf of OpenAI.

But Brockman has previously said that his political giving is intended to support policies favorable to American innovation and the development of artificial intelligence and that his supportwas rooted in OpenAI’s broader mission: “This mission, in my mind, is bigger than companies, bigger than corporate structures.”

The state dinner, scheduled for Thursday, will be one of the most closely watched social events of Xi’s visit, as Trump and Chinese officials seek to manage tensions over trade and AI, among other issues. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese officials have also been discussing a mechanism for notifying each other about major AI-related incidents.

The gathering will bring together senior administration officials, corporate executives and major political donors, including many of the technology leaders whose companies are directly affected by the administration’s China and AI policies.

Many in the AI industry have been urging the administration to take a more hands-on role in AI governance in the lead up to the meetings, including a public call for frontier AI companies to pace their development from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, which Altman and OpenAI endorsed. Altman on Monday alsocalled for the U.S. to take the lead on creating international technical standards for AI safety, a proposal he will present to the U.N. Security Council ahead of the dinner this week.

POLITICO’s Megan Messerly contributed to this report.

item.title: Judge appointed by Trump will oversee news outlets’ lawsuit over White House ban
item.description: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly restored former CNN journalist Jim Acosta’s White House press pass during Trump’s first term.

media:content.media:title: Vaughn Hillyard, a White House correspondent for MS NOW, does a report from near the White House, on Sept. 21, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney and Josh Gerstein
item.dc:contributor: By Kyle Cheney and Josh Gerstein
item.content:encoded:
The emergency lawsuit by three media organizations seeking to lift President Donald Trump’s ban on White House access has landed in the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly.

POLITICO, CNN and MS NOW are asking Kelly, who was appointed to the bench by Trump in his first term, to quickly declare the president’s ban unconstitutional and restore White House access for the organizations’ reporters.

Kelly, who was randomly assigned to the case Monday, set a Tuesday deadline for the Trump administration to respond to the lawsuit and a Wednesday afternoon hearing to consider the organizations’ demand to immediately lift Trump’s ban.

Kelly presided over a similar lawsuit filed by CNN in 2018, after the White House suspended the credentials of correspondent Jim Acosta following a dispute over his actions during a press conference. Kelly held a hearing on the suspension the day after the lawsuit was filed and quickly ordered the White House to restore Acosta’s press pass, citing a lack of due process for the journalist.

White House officials initially insisted they were only temporarily reinstating Acosta’s pass, though they ultimately opted not to take further action against him. Instead, officials issued new policies around conduct at press conferences. With Acosta’s credentials restored, CNN dropped the suit just six days after it was filed.

In a social media post Monday afternoon, Trump took note of that history and seemed to already be bracing for a loss — at least at the initial stage of the case. He also appeared to express regret about appointing Kelly.

“They have drawn a great Judge, for them, a man who ruled in favor of Jim Acosta, who now seems to have disappeared from the Planet. The Judge’s name is Tim Kelly, and he was, sadly, appointed by ‘TRUMP,’” the president wrote on Truth Social. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”

“Why should I have to give ‘access’ to such people? Perhaps Judge Kelly could explain that!” Trump added.

Kelly is perhaps best known for presiding over the six-month jury trial of leaders of the Proud Boys who were charged with seditious conspiracy for their role in the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. After their convictions, Kelly sentenced the group’s national chair, Enrique Tarrio, to a 22-year prison term, the lengthiest for any Jan. 6 defendant. Kelly recently, and reluctantly, ended the Proud Boys case after the Justice Department moved to dismiss the charges in connection with Trump’s grant of clemency to all those charged with Jan. 6-related offenses.

Kelly, 57, graduated from Duke University and earned his law degree at Georgetown. He spent a decade as a federal prosecutor before joining the staff of Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) as a senior counsel focusing on crime and national security. Kelly was nominated by Trump in 2017 and easily won confirmation in the Senate, 94-2, becoming Trump’s first appointee on the district court in Washington.

item.title: News outlets Trump banned from White House file lawsuit
item.description: POLITICO, CNN and MS NOW are seeking a restraining order to restore reporters’ access

media:content.media:title: A reporter looks at his phone in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington on Saturday.

item.dc:creator: By Josh Gerstein and Kyle Cheney
item.dc:contributor: By Josh Gerstein and Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
Three news organizations whose journalists were banned from the White House last week are suing President Donald Trump and three top advisers, calling the abrupt lockout a “direct assault on the First Amendment.”

POLITICO, CNN and MS NOW said in a joint statement Monday that they are bringing the federal lawsuit in a bid to immediately restore access for their reporters, who were denied entry to the White House complex on Saturday and had their credentials confiscated by the Secret Service.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the news organizations said. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

The organizations filed the suit Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, which assigned the case to Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee. The news outlets are asking Kelly to quickly rule Trump’s ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post attacking the news media outlets.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social early Monday. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

The White House’s exclusion of the journalists followed an announcement from Trump on Friday that he was banning reporters for the three outlets “effective immediately.”

Trump’s post Friday was vague about the reasons for the ban, beyond complaining about “constant ‘reporting’” of what he called “FICTION and LIES.” Questioned about the move during an Oval Office photo op, Trump offered few specifics.

“It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it,” Trump said. “They’re smart people, but they purposely write negative news.”

The news organizations, represented by Theodore Boutrous Jr. of law firm Gibson Dunn, are filing suit against Trump, chief of staff Susie Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean Curran. The news outlets argue that the president’s ban violates the Constitution in multiple ways: The abrupt cancellation of White House access without notice violated the organizations’ Fifth Amendment due process and property rights, and the retaliation for the content of their reporting violated their First Amendment rights.

The suit contends that the ban is already “severely impeding” the news organizations’ ability to report on the Trump White House while also causing a chilling effect among other news outlets, who could find themselves similarly locked out if the president deems their coverage “insufficiently favorable.”

“The President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The President has been explicit that this ban is intended to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to intimidate journalists and news organizations covering him and his administration. This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.”

Though long-standing legal precedents permit the White House to restrict journalists’ access to the building, courts have ruled that officials can’t apply those restrictions in ways that discriminate based on viewpoint or content.

Previous efforts by Trump to deny access to specific reporters or news organizations have run into resistance in the courts, although the most recent litigation led to a muddled result.

In 2018, during Trump’s first term, officials suspended the White House hard pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta, with officials contending he kept speaking and clung to the microphone after Trump made clear he was moving on to another reporter. A judge ordered Acosta’s credential restored, citing a murky process surrounding the suspension.

A similar fight played out the following year, after a verbal altercation in the Rose Garden between a freelance journalist for Playboy, Brian Karem, and Trump adviser Sebastian Gorka. A federal judge ordered the White House to return Karem’s credential, concluding that the rules of decorum for such events were not clear enough to provide due process.

Last year, another legal clash erupted after Trump barred the Associated Press from attending East Room events and kicked the wire service out of the White House press pool, the small group of reporters routinely given access to the Oval Office, Air Force One and other sensitive locations frequented by the president. Trump’s action came after the AP refused to adopt Gulf of America, after he signed an executive order renaming the body of water long known as the Gulf of Mexico.

Though a federal district judge sided with the AP, the bulk of his ruling was temporarily put on hold by a panel of the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found the most restricted areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One were not subject to the broader First Amendment protections of the rest of the complex.

“These restricted presidential spaces are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion,” the panel’s majority wrote. “The White House therefore retains discretion to determine, including on the basis of viewpoint, which journalists will be admitted.”

Although the appeals court’s June 2025 ruling was a preliminary one, it allowed Trump to follow through with his attempt to ban the AP from the Oval Office. The AP asked the D.C. Circuit’s full bench to take up the issue, but a majority of the court’s judges declined to do so.

Arguments aimed at a definitive ruling on the AP’s lawsuit took place before a three-judge panel last November. The court has yet to rule.

The D.C. Circuit ruled almost a half-century ago in a case involving Nation magazine reporter Robert Sherrill that journalists can’t be denied access to the White House arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting.

Megan Messerly contributed to this report.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misspelled Theodore Boutrous Jr.'s name.

item.title: ‘He needed to be more empathetic’: GOP donors say Trump missed the mark with latest AI comments
item.description: GOP donors see Trump brushing off public fears about AI as a problem. But they see affordability as an even bigger one.

media:content.media:title: President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally with North Carolina Republican Senate candidate and former RNC Chairman Michael Whatley on September 16 in Gastonia, North Carolina. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

item.dc:creator: By Alex Gangitano
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump dismissed concerns over artificial intelligence this week. Republican donors wish he hadn’t.

Some donors, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly without reprisal, told POLITICO that Trump’s learn-to-love-it broadsides about AI are the latest example of a president who can at times seem out of touch with voter anxieties, likening it to his glibness around cost of living concerns.

Trump has now called both affordability and fears over AI’s disruptive and possibly existentially catastrophic capabilities a “hoax,” putting him on the opposite side of many tech leaders and a growing number of state and national Republicans who believe the government needs new regulations. Trump’s comments came in the wake of renewed concern this week that tech giants are “gambling with our lives,” creating uncontrollable models that could wreak havoc on humanity.

The donor frustration comes amid broader concern that the GOP could lose the House and possibly the Senate in November. Polls look increasingly favorable for Democrats while Trump’s approval rating continues to hover around second-term lows.

“He needed to be more empathetic to the issues that were raised, the concerns and anxieties they provoked amongst American people – because you ignore people’s concerns at your political peril,” a GOP donor said. “If voters feel like you're not responding to their concerns, they often turn to the other party, and so is there a cumulative effect?”

A White House official said Trump has clearly articulated that his goal is to “ensure continued American dominance in AI and other cutting-edge technologies” and that the policy of the Trump administration is to sustain AI dominance over China.

“The hoax that President Trump is referring to is that Democrats are using AI concern as a way to score points weeks before the midterms election, just like the hoax that the world would be extinguished by climate change,” the person said.

About two out of three Americans say there is at least a “moderate” risk that advanced AI could destroy humanity, with majorities across parties, genders and age groups holding that view, according to a new POLITICO poll.

A second GOP donor said Trump’s focus on maintaining AI dominance over China is “admirable” but there needs to be a better effort to sell the vision to the public.

“The polling will be tough to move,” the donor said. “It requires close messaging coordination between both industries and the White House that appears to be lacking. Without it, while AI may not kill us all, it might kill vulnerable Republicans this year.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman amplified the existential concerns this week, warning that the pace of development needs to slow.

Trump ally and mega GOP donor Elon Musk said Amodei“is right.” And Palantir CEO Alex Karp on Thursdaycalled for AI to be nationalized because of the technology’s “unlimited risks.”

One MAGA Inc. donor said that Trump may have intended to allay fears and downplay the most extreme scenarios but ultimately the president failed to show an understanding of the broader concern.

“In his mind, he was rationalizing a method in which to calm people down. And then what does Karp do today? ‘Oh my God, it's so damn bad. We should nationalize it,’” the donor said.

“Depending upon how they took what Trump said, I think a lot of [voters] might have thought, ‘Hey, you know, it doesn't sound like he's really given this much consideration,’” the donor added. “I'd rather have somebody in there that would take it more seriously because they need to.’”

But for many donors, their concerns over how the White House is — or isn’ t— handling AI pale in comparison to the worsening economic picture that many believe will determine the election.

Mortgage rates are at their highest since January 2025. Diesel fuel, which fuels huge swaths of American industry, is at record highs and that could further increase food prices. And the average price for a gallon of gasoline is $4.47, according to AAA, up 10 percent in the last month.

Only 19 percent of voters approve of Trump’s handling of inflation and the cost of living and 20 percent of voters approve of his handling of gas prices, according to a new Marquette University Law School poll.

“Trump’s bombastic bullishness on AI safety is not the problem – voters aren’t focused on AI beyond data centers – it’s the cost of diesel and lack of progress in Iran that leave his approval sub-40 and create a serious drag on Republican candidates in a referendum midterm,” said a leading AI lobbyist who has donated to multiple Republican Senate campaigns.

Five GOP-held Senate seats are ranked as toss ups by the nonpartisan handicapper Cook Political Report, including in states that Trump won by double digits in 2024, such as Alaska, Iowa and Texas. In the House, 16 GOP-held seats are ranked as toss ups, compared with five Democrat-held seats.

Those vulnerable Republicans are feeling the pressure from affordability above all other issues, said one former Trump administration official.

“When I talk to members, it’s really about affordability. It’s about gas prices, diesel prices. They’re pissed about the beef thing,” the person said. “Maybe you have a local data center issue and you’ll probably get ads but I just don’t know if the biggest questions—should we be embracing AI full throated or no— is going to really matter in these elections.”

Vice President JD Vance and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries focused on cost of living issues, not AI, in meetings with their respective parties on the Hill this week.

Still, despite AI being lower on the list of concerns compared with pocketbook issues, donors want Trump to give voters’ anxiety over the fast-paced technology more attention.

“People are worried about cost, farmers are worried about grain prices, cattle prices. People are worried about, in Michigan, the cross-border trade. And you’re talking about dismissing people’s fears about jobs and their economy,” the first GOP donor said. “That is not the recipe for reassembling a winning coalition.”
